name: Platelet-rich fibrin matrix (PRFM)

card.summary: A platelet concentrate made from the patient's own blood that forms a fibrin scaffold, used in cosmetic and facial rejuvenation procedures to support skin and tissue healing.
card.aka: Platelet-rich fibrin matrix; Fibrinet PRFM; platelet-rich fibrin (related)
card.note: Cosmetic evidence is mostly small studies; PRFM is an autologous procedure done by clinicians.

quick.overview:
Platelet-rich fibrin matrix is an autologous blood product: blood is drawn from the patient, processed to concentrate platelets in a fibrin scaffold, and returned to the face as a gel-like volumizing and rejuvenating treatment. It is a cousin of platelet-rich plasma (PRP), the better-known facial treatment.

Proponents use it for skin quality, fine lines and soft-tissue fill. Reviews describe growth factors released from platelets as the proposed mechanism, and say stronger studies are needed to define results and best use of each preparation.
quick.how: In general terms, a clinician draws a small blood sample, processes it into a matrix and places it in or under the skin of areas such as the under-eyes or cheeks. Sessions are done in clinics, and the matrix has also been used in dental and orthopedic procedures.
quick.risks: Because the material comes from the patient's own blood, allergic reaction is not the main concern; reported issues with injections in general include bruising, swelling and infection risk from the procedure. Reviews describe cosmetic evidence as thin and recommend careful understanding of differences between preparations.

lead: Platelet-rich fibrin matrix (PRFM) is one of several autologous platelet concentrates. A review sorts these into four families by leukocyte content and fibrin structure, listing pure platelet-rich fibrin, such as Fibrinet PRFM, as its own category beside PRP and leukocyte-rich variants.[1] Compared with a PRP gel that releases growth factors quickly, fibrin membranes are described as releasing them over a longer period.[1]

For appearance, PRFM is used in facial rejuvenation and tissue fill. A review in Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics notes that platelet preparations, including platelet-rich plasma and PRFM, have been used to improve wound healing, recovery time and cosmetic results, with released growth factors considered the likely active agents and calls for more robust studies.[2]
Most published PRFM trials are in dentistry and orthopedics rather than aesthetics, including periodontal defects, implants and rotator cuff repair.[3][4]

chain: Patient's blood is processed into a platelet-rich fibrin matrix
Matrix is placed in or under facial skin
Growth factors support tissue repair and mild fill
angle.text: Clinics offer PRFM for skin rejuvenation and gentle volume, for example under the eyes. Platelet growth factors are the proposed route to firmer, healthier-looking skin.

infobox: Facial rejuvenation, dental and orthopedic surgery

paras: Platelet concentrates are autologous products with higher than baseline platelet counts, intended to enhance healing.[1] Platelet-rich fibrin more broadly is prepared by centrifuging blood without an anticoagulant so a fibrin clot forms; it is used mainly as a scaffold in oral and maxillofacial surgery.[5]

Facial rejuvenation uses platelet preparations including PRP and PRFM for skin rejuvenation and tissue fill, and reviewers note that different processing methods yield preparations with different properties.[2] A systematic appraisal of PRP in facial rejuvenation, which is the related and more studied technique, found 36 studies in 3,172 patients, with a median of 27.5 patients per study, reflecting how small aesthetic trials tend to be.[6]

A prospective randomized study examined PRFM on rotator cuff tendon healing,[4] and randomized trials have tested it in periodontal defects with bone graft material.[3] An editorial commentary asked whether PRFM was 'for real', reflecting debate over its benefits in orthopedics.[7] No randomized trials of PRFM specifically for facial appearance are cited here.
